Big enquiry: Was the peace settlement a just response to the First World War, or did it sow the seeds of future conflict? Use different perspectives and precise facts; avoid simplistic blame.
3.1
Allied reactions · pages 16–17

How satisfied were the Allies with Versailles?

Britain, France and the USA reacted differently; within each country, public opinion often differed from leaders’ private concerns.

Britain · public opinion

Years of anti-German propaganda, wartime deaths and food shortages made many people demand punishment. British election slogans in 1918 promised to make Germany pay. Lloyd George was welcomed home as a hero, although people differed on whether the peace was harsh enough.

France · public opinion

France suffered invasion, ruined land and massive casualties. French people welcomed a reduced German army, a demilitarised Rhineland, Saar coal rights and reparations. Some wanted Germany crippled or broken up, and thought the treaty was too lenient.

USA · public opinion

Many Americans regarded the terms as unfair and wanted isolationism. Republican opponents argued the settlement did not follow Wilson’s Fourteen Points; the US Senate did not ratify the treaty, and the USA stayed outside the League of Nations.

Compare the leaders with their publics

CountryLeader: achievedLeader: concernsPublic / domestic politics
BritainNaval superiority, mandates, reparationsDamaging trade; resentment; potential new warWanted Germany to pay; celebrated Lloyd George
FranceGermany weakened; Rhineland demilitarised; Saar coal; reparationsNo independent Rhineland; feared future German recoveryMany demanded more severe measures; Clemenceau lost office in 1920
USALeague of Nations established; some national independenceTreaty too harsh; incomplete self-determinationRepublican Senate rejected ratification; isolationism

Read a cartoon, not just the caption

1 · IdentifyWho made it? Where and when?
2 · ObserveWhat symbols, labels and characters appear?
3 · InferWhat argument is the artist making?
4 · ContextWhich treaty debates explain that viewpoint?

British cartoon: a child labelled “1940 Class” suggests another generation may be drawn into war. American cartoon: a senator fears the League might drag the USA into foreign conflict. Neither cartoon is a neutral record of what would happen.

Exam Tip · inference (4 marks): Identify a clear message, quote or describe an exact detail, and explain it with relevant context. A cartoonist’s prediction is evidence of an attitude, not proof of the future.

3.2
German response · pages 18–19

The German reaction to Versailles

Germany called Versailles a Diktat. Resentment became a major source of political tension in the new Weimar Republic.

Why Germans were outraged

Many had been told Germany was winning. The Kaiser abdicated on 9 November 1918, and the armistice followed on 11 November. Germany had not negotiated the final terms and called the Treaty a Diktat. The blockade and wartime shortages increased anger.

The new democratic government faced the impossible choice: sign a hated settlement or risk renewed fighting.

Political consequences

Opponents called signatories “November Criminals” and spread the false “stab-in-the-back” myth, blaming civilians and the new Republic rather than military defeat. Anger contributed to distrust of Weimar democracy, extremist movements and attempted putsches.

Key distinction: propaganda claims are not reliable explanations for Germany’s military defeat.

Chain of consequences · the political and economic crisis

War defeat, 1918→Diktat and resentment, 1919→1923 Ruhr occupation→Passive resistance + money printing→Hyperinflation

Germany missed a reparations delivery in 1923. French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr; the German government supported passive resistance and printed money to pay workers, contributing to catastrophic hyperinflation. The crisis cannot be attributed to the Treaty alone without explaining the intervening decisions.

Interactive timeline · select a turning point

Exam Tip · account (8 marks): Explain a sequence: harsh settlement → political anger → instability and/or the reparations crisis → Ruhr and hyperinflation. Show how one event contributed to the next.

3.3
Debating fairness · pages 20–21

How fair was the wider peace settlement?

A strong judgement weighs the settlement’s effects against the genuine security needs of war-torn countries.

Arguments that the peace was unfair

Diktat: Germans were excluded from negotiations. War guilt: the causes of the First World War were complex, but Article 231 assigned responsibility for losses and damage to Germany and its allies. Territorial losses: the treaty separated millions of Germans from Germany and removed resources. Disarmament: many Germans feared vulnerability. Reparations: a financial and symbolic burden.

Arguments defending the peacemakers

The war devastated Europe, and victors expected compensation and security. Harsh terms were not unusual after defeat; Germany itself had imposed severe terms on Soviet Russia at Brest-Litovsk (1918). The collapse of several empires made territorial settlement difficult. Later, some historians noted that Germany recovered considerable economic and military strength, suggesting the treaty was not permanently crippling.

Fair or unfair? · interactive evidence

For Grade 8–9, evaluate both the moral fairness of terms and their ability to produce lasting stability.

Exam Tip · source usefulness (12 marks): For EACH source, assess (1) what it reveals, (2) whether contextual knowledge supports or limits it, and (3) how its author, date and purpose shape its value. A biased source can still be highly useful evidence of contemporary resentment.

3.4
Other peace treaties · pages 22–23

How were Germany’s allies treated?

The peace settlement redrew the map of Europe — but borders, minorities and enforcement remained controversial.

Versailles was not the only settlement. Germany’s former allies and the broken empires were dealt with in separate treaties, creating new states and new disputes.

Explore five peace treaties

TreatyDefeated stateSettlementProblems / impact
Saint-Germain · 10 Sep 1919AustriaTerritory to Italy, Romania, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia; 30,000 soldiers; no union with GermanyEconomic dislocation; Austria lost much industrial capacity; new minority disputes
Neuilly · 27 Nov 1919BulgariaTerritory to Yugoslavia, Greece and Romania; army 20,000; no conscription; reparationsLosses, but also some territory gained from Turkey
Trianon · 4 Jun 1920HungaryLarge territorial losses; army 35,000 under standard reference accounts (textbook lists 30,000); no conscriptionEconomic difficulties and ethnic Hungarians left outside Hungary
Sèvres · 10 Aug 1920Ottoman Empire / TurkeySevere territorial losses; restricted military; straits subject to international conditionsResistance and war: treaty never fully enforced
Lausanne · Jul 1923TurkeyRevised settlement; greater control and sovereignty; reparations abandonedShowed a harsh settlement could be overturned
Careful factual check: your textbook prints a 30,000-man limit for Hungary under Trianon. Standard historical accounts commonly give 35,000; we flag this discrepancy rather than silently teaching conflicting figures. For GCSE, understand the point: severe disarmament and loss of territory.

Eastern Europe: more states, not simple solutions

Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia emerged or expanded. Many had mixed ethnic populations, disputed borders and economic problems. The Polish Corridor gave Poland sea access but separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany. The Allies hoped smaller states would provide a buffer against Germany and Bolshevik Russia.

Why Lausanne mattered

Turkish nationalist resistance led by Mustafa Kemal overturned the Sèvres settlement, and the Allies replaced it with Lausanne in 1923. This illustrated difficulties enforcing treaties when a defeated state resisted successfully, and gave critics reason to question the security of other settlements.

Exam Tip · breadth of evidence: Use specific treaty names and consequences to test whether the whole peace settlement brought stability. Do not claim that every new state was immediately unsuccessful.

3.5
Peacemakers’ outcomes · pages 24–25

To what extent did the Big Three achieve their aims?

Each leader achieved important aims but was forced to accept significant disappointments.

Did the Big Three achieve their aims?

LeaderWhat went their wayWhere aims were frustrated
Clemenceau · FranceGerman military reduced; Rhineland demilitarised; reparations; Saar coal for 15 yearsGermany not broken up; Rhineland not independent; terms judged too soft by some French voters
Wilson · USALeague of Nations created; some new nations gained independenceUS Senate rejected Treaty and League membership; self-determination selective; Wilson disliked punitive terms
Lloyd George · BritainGerman navy reduced; colonies became mandates; Britain received economic and strategic advantagesReparations threatened German trade; harshness encouraged resentment; fear of another war

Historical judgement builder

Choose which leader seems most satisfied — then make the case using two achievements, one limitation, and a reasoned overall judgement.

Exam Tip · 16 marks + 4 SPaG: Take a position, explain evidence both for and against the claim, then weigh the importance of different aims. A judgement must compare what the leaders most wanted, not simply count successes.

ContentWhat exactly does each source say or depict?
ContextWhich historical knowledge helps explain or test it?
ProvenanceWho created it, when and for what audience?
Utility judgementHow useful is it for this enquiry, and with what limitations?

A political cartoon may be partisan yet useful evidence of contemporary opinion. Do not reject a source only because it is biased.
